answer.rationale: With 14 days to expiry, no auto-renew, and the line at 94% of committed volume with zero buffer, a vendor switch (memory_c2) is the highest TCO-risk path despite its historical unit-cost gains; any onboarding slip now stops the line. Deferring past expiry creates a coverage gap, and memory_c5's deferral worked only for a non-critical service. The lowest-risk route to the mandated 18% cut is renegotiating with the incumbent at renewal: memory_c1 shows renewal keeps integration and deliveries stable, memory_c4 shows benchmarking at renewal moved the incumbent on both price and payment terms, and memory_c6 shows a multi-year commitment unlocks volume pricing without narrowing scope. Combining benchmark leverage with a longer term is the most credible way to approach the 18% target while holding delivery risk flat. I am verifying memory_c4 because the entire cost-cut thesis rests on whether renewal-time renegotiation genuinely recovered margin. Adding a second source (memory_c3) remains valuable but is the next-cycle decision, since capacity allows only one move and the expiring contract is the binding constraint.
